rows.title: NuclearLang — Hard rules
rows.summary: 12. Node.js/Express is postponed by the user: do not touch it until asked.
body: 12. Node.js/Express is postponed by the user: do not touch it until asked.
13. **A product is made with the tools** ([ADR-platform-0004](docs/03-adr/0004-products-are-made-with-the-tools.md)).
A product is any software made from Nuclear (an app, a backend, the website, an example). Its code is Nuclear,
its target code comes from the transpiler, its standard parts from `nuclear new`/`gen`/`make` and the MCP
server, its libraries from `nuclear add`. No agent writes target code for a feature or migrates code of a
native dialect (React, Node.js, Python/FastAPI, Dart) into Nuclear by hand. By hand outside Nuclear only when
strictly necessary: say so, and record the missing capability in the roadmap of the tool that should do it.

rows.title: NuclearLang — Hard rules
rows.summary: pending.
body: pending. A dialect's reference holds the real Nuclear → target equivalences, checked by `spec-check` (0 problems).
6. **Every new diagnostic code is documented** in `nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/diagnostics.md`; every dialect
word in its `docs.toml`.
7. **Each project documents itself, in short files.** A change is done when its tests are green and the documents
of the project it touches say it, in the same change, and the knowledge base follows
([docs/05-standards/coding.md](docs/05-standards/coding.md)). Pending work is the project's
`docs/01-product/roadmap.md`: a done item is deleted, half-done work is recorded the moment it is left. No file
lists the state of the whole platform, and no document describes another project.
8. **Quality first**: always the right solution, even when it costs more. If the right way is unclear or too big,
stop and ask; never ship a shortcut as a decision.
9. **Nuclear first**: every new piece of the platform is written in Nuclear (with the framework when a platform
fits, with a language dialect when none does). Another language only where Nuclear cannot be the source yet.
10. **No commits unless the user asks**; commits only in the user's name, with no co-author line.
11. `CodeBuilder/` is teaching material only: never in references, context or code.

rows.title: NuclearLang — Hard rules
rows.summary: 1. English everywhere: code, comments, diagnostics, the tools' output, dialects, examples, documents.
body: 1. **English everywhere**: code, comments, diagnostics, the tools' output, dialects, examples, documents. The
exceptions are localization data and the tests of unicode. **The chat with the user is always in Spanish.**
2. **The parser does not change per dialect.** Framework words, shortcuts and imports are data of the dialects.
Rust decides *what* is emitted; the dialect decides *how*.
3. **A dialect only changes the output.** The same Nuclear code is written once and built for every dialect of
its platform; a `.nuc` never bends its naming or its syntax to make a dialect easier.
4. **Three platforms; the dialects only change the language underneath.** A platform is what the user and the
agent write, identical for every dialect of it. The Nuclear of a project never changes when its dialect changes
(the one exception: code that uses a dialect's type definitions). The standard library is Nuclear's own; a
target's library name in platform code, references or examples is a bug. A platform's reference names no
dialect. Kinds are Nuclear's libraries: an extension kind is a package of TOML, templates and a runtime, never
a change to the compiler.
5. **A reference holds only final rules** (`docs/07-reference/` of a project): no question, no history, nothing

rows.title: NuclearLang
rows.summary: A minimal base language for AI agents and people.
body: A minimal base language for AI agents and people. A Rust transpiler turns `.nuc` into other technologies through
**declarative dialects** (TOML and templates loaded at run time), one way only (`.nuc` → `.ts` / `.dart` / `.py`).
Website: [nuclearlang.github.io](https://nuclearlang.github.io); repository: `nuclearlang/lang`.
The language comes with its framework, as Rust has Actix: three platforms (`web`, `mobile`, `backend`), each
written once in Nuclear and built by its dialects. Vision: [docs/00-context/vision.md](docs/00-context/vision.md).
One git repository. Each folder below is a **project** that documents itself. Read this file, then the `AGENTS.md`
of the one project the task touches, then only the document whose line there matches the task
([docs/README.md](docs/README.md) is the standard every project follows).

rows.title: NuclearLang — The golden rule
rows.summary: fast as an expert's, instant transpilation, minimal readable Nuclear.
body: **Performance, speed and readability of the syntax**, for the base language and every dialect: generated code as
fast as an expert's, instant transpilation, minimal readable Nuclear.

body: - Any package of the target is used through Nuclear (ADR-lang-0008). A name called like its package is imported by name
(`from tqdm import tqdm`, `import { nanoid } from 'nanoid'`; before, as the package itself); `index.json` has
`defaults`, a package's default export (`import dayjs from 'dayjs'`), which `gen.js` now describes; `config.nuc`
takes a name that is not an identifier (`"date-fns@^4.1.0"`); `[project.manifest.advice]`; `nuclear defs` reads the
packages of the project it runs in; `gen.py --distribution` and `gen.js --package`; `defs.dart` skips the library of
a plugin the app has not enabled (it failed every `flutter add` there). A member of a module (`np.max(list)` after
`use numpy as np`) or of a library's function or object (`lodash.map(...)`) is the library's own: it was rewritten
as the member of Nuclear's library with that name (`_max(np)`).
- First public version.

- `STATUS.md` holds only what is left to do (half done, untested, pending) and keeps no log: what a task did is written in the documentation of its area, and no file is made to hold history (`AGENTS.md` rule 6, `docs/context/workflow.md`); the start hook (`tools/context/check.sh session`) warns when the file is over 40 KB.

rows.summary: Unreleased
body: - ADR-installer-0002: the AI services come with the installer. Every release archive carries the code of the Smart Graph and the Nuclear Developer with its knowledge base (`ai/`, `tools/release/stage.sh`); the installers end with their set-up (`nuclear-builder setup`: a profile for the machine, the services at every login), bring a machine already set up to date without questions, and take `--no-ai` and `--profile <id>` (`-NoAi`, `-AiProfile` on Windows); `--uninstall` removes the services; `./install.sh --ai` is the same set-up over the working tree. `docs/ai/setup.md`; the release workflow clones the three AI repositories.

rows.title: NuclearLang — Why
rows.summary: Why
body: - Agents spend most of their tokens on code that is always the same; in Nuclear only the business logic is written.
- One way to write each thing, errors that come with their fix, type definitions so nobody invents an API.
- One way only (`.nuc` → target); it never replaces the target's own tools. [Vision](docs/00-context/vision.md).

rows.title: Domain model — Invariants
rows.summary: uses a dialect's type definitions (`numpy` exists only in Python), which ties that code to that dialect.
body: - INV-001: The Nuclear code of a project never changes when its dialect changes. The one exception is code that
uses a dialect's type definitions (`numpy` exists only in Python), which ties that code to that dialect.
- INV-002: The parser does not change per dialect.
- INV-003: A target's library name (`push`, `len`, `toUpperCase`) in platform code, references or examples is a bug.
- INV-004: A platform's reference names no dialect.

rows.title: Domain model — Rules
rows.summary: `nuclear.toml` and a language dialect.
body: - R-001: A project names a platform and a dialect in its `config.nuc`; a library or a command line tool has a
`nuclear.toml` and a language dialect.
- R-002: A framework dialect implements exactly the kinds of its platform's contract; the loader refuses one that
adds or lacks a kind.
- R-003: The standard library is Nuclear's own; every dialect translates it.
- R-004: Kinds and features may differ between platforms, never between the dialects of one platform.

rows.title: Glossary
rows.summary: Glossary
body: | Term | Meaning | Do not say | Where |
| Nuclear | The base language: what a `.nuc` file is written in. | "NuclearLang code" for a dialect's output | `nuclearlang/` |
| Dialect | The data (TOML, templates) that says how Nuclear is written in one target. It never changes what the Nuclear code is. | "backend dialect" for a platform | `nuclearlang/dialects/` |
| Language dialect | A dialect of a target language: `python`, `typescript`, `dart`, `nodejs`. | | `nuclearlang/dialects/<language>/` |

| Framework dialect | A dialect that writes a platform of the framework in a target framework: `fastapi`, `nestjs`, `flutter`, `react`. It extends a language dialect. | | `nuclearlang/dialects/<language>/frameworks/<name>/` |

| Synapsis, the framework | What the language comes with for applications: kinds, decorators, components, `config.nuc` (`synapsis(platform, dialect)`), plugins, tests. Its commands are `nuclear`'s. | | `nuclear-synapsis-framework/` |
| Platform | `web`, `mobile` or `backend`: what the user and the agent write, identical for every dialect of it. | "dialect" for a platform | `nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/<platform>/` |
| Contract | A platform's `platform.toml`: the kinds, decorators and plugins every dialect of it implements. | | each platform |

rows.title: Glossary
rows.summary: Glossary
body: | Kind | The word that opens a declaration (`model`, `usecase`, `screen`): a library of Nuclear. Native kinds are a platform's; extension kinds come in a package. | "class" | the contract, kind packages |
| Type definitions (defs) | The public API of a target's library, by package and version, so names are known and imports are written. | | `nuclearlang/dialects/<language>/defs/` |
| Reference | The normative text of a project (`docs/07-reference/`): a language's rules, a dialect's equivalences. | "spec" (a spec is a change being built: `docs/04-specs/`) | each project |
| Brief | The short sheet an agent reads before writing Nuclear for a dialect or a platform. | | `docs/07-reference/brief/` |
| The Smart Graph | The local, private knowledge base every agent reads. | "the RAG" in documents | `nuclear-graph-storage/` |
| Shelf, row, card | The graph's storage: a shelf holds typed rows; a card is what a search gives back. | | the graph |
| The Developer | The local agents (coder, tester, planner...). | | `nuclear-agents/nuclear_developer/` |
| `nuclear` | The one command line tool: the compiler's commands and the framework's (`new`, `make`, `gen`, `run`, `test`...). | "the `synapsis` command" | `tools/cli/` |
| Nuclear Builder | The pipeline tool of the editors: command `nuclear-builder`, runs in `.nuclear/builder/`. | | `extensions/tools/nuclear-builder/` |

rows.title: Vision — Constraints
rows.summary: Constraints
body: - Technical: the parser never changes per dialect; Rust decides what is emitted, the dialect how.
- Of the user: local models of at most 3B parameters (`ADR-platform-0003`); Node.js/Express is postponed.

rows.title: Vision — Non-goals
rows.summary: Non-goals
body: - Reading or converting target code into Nuclear.
- Records, operator overloading, pattern `switch` of Dart 3 (`nuclearlang/docs/02-architecture/limits.md`).
- Replacing the target's own tools: Flutter's command still builds and runs; `nuclear` drives it.

rows.title: Vision — Problem
rows.summary: An AI agent that writes an application spends most of its tokens on code that is always the same: the wiring of a framework, imports, serialization, state, tests.
body: An AI agent that writes an application spends most of its tokens on code that is always the same: the wiring of a
framework, imports, serialization, state, tests. It also invents APIs that do not exist. People who work with
agents read and review that code.
NuclearLang is a minimal base language for agents and the people who work with them: the fastest to write and to
read, with the fewest tokens. It is not compiled to machine code. A transpiler written in Rust turns `.nuc` into
the code of another technology through **declarative dialects** (TOML and templates loaded at run time), one way
only: `.nuc` → `.ts` / `.dart` / `.py`. It never reads target code.
The language comes with its framework, Synapsis (`nuclear-synapsis-framework/`), as Rust has

Actix: three platforms (`web`, `mobile`, `backend`) written once in Nuclear. The framework brings the architecture; in Nuclear only the business logic is written, and the transpiler generates the rest.
Open source, in the spirit of Rust, Deno, Gleam and Bun.

rows.title: Vision — The golden rule
rows.summary: (`ADR-lang-0001`): generated code as fast as an expert's in the target, instant transpilation, minimal and readable Nuclear.
body: **Performance, speed and readability of the syntax**, for the base language and every dialect
(`ADR-lang-0001`): generated code as fast as an expert's in the target, instant transpilation, minimal and
readable Nuclear. A rule, kind or shortcut that breaks one of the three is rejected.

rows.title: Vision — Users
rows.summary: diagnostics with fixes, a reference they can follow, type definitions so they do not invent APIs.
body: - AI coding agents (Claude, Codex, OpenCode, the local agents): few tokens, one way to write each thing, clear
diagnostics with fixes, a reference they can follow, type definitions so they do not invent APIs.
- Developers of applications: write the business logic only; a project that builds, tests and runs with one
command; editor support like the target's own.
- Authors of dialects: add a target or a framework without touching Rust: data files, templates, a contract, tests.

rows.title: Product requirements: the NuclearLang platform — Functional requirements
rows.summary: Functional requirements
body: | ID | Requirement | Project |

| FR-01 | A base language: header and block, 2-space indentation, values everywhere, modules, inheritance, generics, `Result<E, T>` with automatic propagation, aliases, destructuring, generators, cascades | `nuclearlang/` |
| FR-02 | A file or a project of several files is transpiled to TypeScript, Dart and Python | `nuclearlang/` |
| FR-03 | Dialects are data: inheritance, templates, kinds, decorators, options, keywords, a contract | `nuclearlang/`, each dialect |
| FR-04 | Type definitions per package and version: auto-imports, inherited members, the API for the language server and the agents | each dialect |
| FR-05 | Diagnostics with codes, positions and fixes, as text and as JSON | `nuclearlang/` |
| FR-06 | A language server: diagnostics, completion, hover, signature help, rename, metrics, documentation | `nuclearlang/` |
| FR-07 | Extensions for VS Code, JetBrains and Zed | `extensions/` |
| FR-08 | A framework with three platforms (web, mobile, backend), each written once and built by its dialects | `nuclear-synapsis-framework/` |
| FR-09 | One command line tool: new, make, gen, build, run, test, devices, packages | `tools/cli/` |
| FR-10 | `.nuc` is debugged through the target's debugger | `nuclearlang/`, `extensions/` |
| FR-11 | Agents are supported: a brief, a skill, files for a project, an evaluation | `tools/cli/` |

rows.title: Product requirements: the NuclearLang platform — Non-functional requirements

body: | ID | Requirement |
| NFR-01 | Generated code passes the target's analyzer without warnings (`flutter analyze`, `tsc --strict`, `pyright --strict`) |
| NFR-02 | A build with no change takes about 40 ms; a project build about 20 ms in release |
| NFR-03 | The parser never changes per dialect; Rust decides what is emitted, the dialect how |
| NFR-04 | Everything in English (`ADR-platform-0001`) |
| NFR-05 | Every diagnostic code is documented; every dialect word is documented for the editor |
| NFR-06 | Errors over magic: no inferred parameters, no hoisting; explicit beats implicit when in doubt |
| NFR-07 | A local model has at most 3B parameters (`ADR-platform-0003`) |

rows.title: Architecture of the platform
rows.summary: How the projects fit together.
rows.body: How the projects fit together. What is inside each is in that project's `docs/02-architecture/`.

rows.title: Architecture of the platform — Borders that hold
rows.summary: code generator and the devices as libraries; what it needs from a platform comes from the dialect's data (`[toolchain]`), never from a name written in Rust.
body: - An extension talks to the language server only through the LSP protocol and its documented `nuclear/*` requests.
- One command line tool, `nuclear`: the compiler's commands and the framework's. It uses the compiler crates, the
code generator and the devices as libraries; what it needs from a platform comes from the
dialect's data (`[toolchain]`), never from a name written in Rust.
- A framework dialect lives with its language; the platform it implements lives with the framework. Neither
describes the other.
- The local agents reach the graph and the compiler only through the graph's client and the tools it gives them.
- The MCP server is a Nuclear project of its own (`python` dialect); it reaches the graph through the graph's
package and runs `nuclear` for a project's commands.
- The website (`website/`) reads the reference and the guides of every project at build time; no page is written
in it.

rows.title: Architecture of the platform — From `.nuc` to the target
rows.summary: .nuc text the dialect's *.toml (+ its type definitions) │ 1 LEXER text → tokens (INDENT/DEDENT) │ loaded at run time: │ 2 PARSER tokens → AST (no format) │ inheritance, merge, validation │ 3 RESOLVER block scope, undefined names, ▼ │ implicit this, const/let, async ◄── Dialect: kinds, shortcuts,…
body: .nuc text                                   the dialect's *.toml (+ its type definitions)
│ 1 LEXER     text → tokens (INDENT/DEDENT)        │ loaded at run time:
│ 2 PARSER    tokens → AST (no format)             │ inheritance, merge, validation
│ 3 RESOLVER  block scope, undefined names,        ▼
│             implicit this, const/let, async ◄── Dialect: kinds, shortcuts, auto-imports
│ 4 EMITTER   AST → the dialect's templates  ◄── [syntax] [types] [operators] [options]
.ts / .dart / .py text  (+ a line map target → .nuc for debuggers)
Each stage knows only the one before. Diagnostics accumulate in all of them and come out as text or JSON.

rows.title: Architecture of the platform — Qualities and how they are reached
rows.summary: Qualities and how they are reached
body: | Quality | How |
| The same Nuclear on every dialect of a platform | the platform's contract, checked by the loader |
| Generated code as an expert writes it | the references' equivalences are the transpiler's real output (`spec-check`), the targets' analyzers in strict mode |
| Agents do not invent | type definitions, diagnostics with fixes, the briefs, the Smart Graph |
| Fast builds | data is read only when needed; a project build is incremental |

rows.title: Architecture of the platform — Rules of the design
rows.summary: 1. The lexer turns indentation into tokens; inside `( ) [ ] { }` it emits none.
body: 1. The lexer turns indentation into tokens; inside `( ) [ ] { }` it emits none.
2. The AST has no format; every node keeps its position for errors and the language server.
3. The parser is generic: a dialect's words arrive as data in a declaration's header.
4. The transpiler knows no target language: TypeScript, Dart and Python are dialects like any other.
5. Data before code: dialects, shortcuts and imports are files read at run time; the same files feed the command
line tool, the language server and the MCP server.
6. Imports are decided after emitting, from the words of the generated code.

rows.summary: editors extensions/{vscode,jetbrains,zed} + extensions/tools/<tool> │ LSP protocol │ run tools nuclearlang/crates/nuclear-lsp tools/cli: `nuclear` tools/mcp: `nuclear-mcp` │ ├ tools/code_generator (nuclear-codegen) │ └ device-emulators (nuclear-devices) │ Rust API (crates) │ compiler…
body: editors      extensions/{vscode,jetbrains,zed}  +  extensions/tools/<tool>
│ LSP protocol                      │ run
tools        nuclearlang/crates/nuclear-lsp      tools/cli: `nuclear`         tools/mcp: `nuclear-mcp`
│                             ├ tools/code_generator (nuclear-codegen)
│                             └ device-emulators (nuclear-devices)
│ Rust API (crates)                 │
compiler     nuclearlang/crates: nuclear-syntax → nuclear-transpile ← nuclear-dialect, nuclear-diag
│ data: TOML, templates, type definitions

│ implement

AI           nuclear-graph-storage (what every agent reads)  ←  nuclear-agents/nuclear_developer
delivery     installer/, website/ (the documentation site)

rows.title: How code is written here — A change is done when
rows.summary: 1. `cargo test` and `cargo clippy --all-targets` are green.
body: 1. `cargo test` and `cargo clippy --all-targets` are green. Output changed: `UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 cargo test`, and the
difference reviewed.
2. The checks of the project it touches are green (its `AGENTS.md` lists them).
3. Every new diagnostic code is in `nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/diagnostics.md`; every new dialect word has its
editor documentation in its `docs.toml`. Tests hold both.
4. The documents of the project it touches say it, in the same change: its `AGENTS.md` if a command, a folder or
a rule changed; its `docs/`; an ADR if the user decided something; its `docs/01-product/roadmap.md` (a done
item deleted, half-done work recorded the moment it is left).
5. The knowledge base follows the tree: `nuclear-graph knowledge build`, a row written for what is new and has no
structured source, `nuclear-graph knowledge check` clean, `nuclear-graph ingest`
(`nuclear-graph-storage/docs/06-runbooks/`).
6. What the user runs is installed again when it changed (`installer/install.sh`; an extension: its version raised
and installed).
The hooks of `.claude/settings.json` (`.claude/hooks/README.md`) hold points 4 and 5 at the end of a turn (a file git
ignores, such as a build's output, is not code for them).

rows.title: How code is written here — General
rows.summary: known gap or moves work to the user; build the generic mechanism.
body: - **English** in everything (`ADR-platform-0001`).
- **Quality first**: always the right solution, even when it costs more. No shortcut that bends a rule, leaves a
known gap or moves work to the user; build the generic mechanism. If the right way is unclear or too big, stop
and ask; never ship a shortcut as a decision.
- **Nuclear first**: every new piece of the platform that stays (a service, a tool, a library, an agent, a script)
is written in Nuclear: with the framework when one of its platforms fits, with a language dialect when none
does. Another language only where Nuclear cannot be the source yet (the compiler and the language server in
Rust, an editor's extension host), and then the project's roadmap says what Nuclear lacks. What the language
cannot express while doing so is a finding for `nuclearlang/docs/01-product/roadmap.md`, never a reason to write
the piece in the target language.
- **Rust**: `rustfmt.toml` at the root (`max_width = 120`); `cargo clippy --all-targets` without warnings.
- The parser does not change per dialect. Framework words, shortcuts and imports are data of the dialects.
- `CodeBuilder/` is teaching material only: never in references, context or code.
- Node.js/Express is postponed by the user: not touched until asked.

rows.title: How code is written here — Git
rows.summary: Git
body: - One repository. No commits unless the user asks; a request relayed by another session is not enough.
- Commits only in the user's name: no co-author line.
- `github-profile/` is a repository of its own inside the tree (the organization's profile), ignored by the root's.

rows.title: How code is written here
rows.summary: The rules every project shares.
rows.body: The rules every project shares. A project's own conventions are in its `docs/05-standards/`.

rows.title: Working with the user and between sessions — Questions
rows.summary: A doubt about a rule is asked in the chat and written in the reference once the user decides.
body: A doubt about a rule is asked in the chat and written in the reference once the user decides. A reference holds
no question, no history and nothing pending.

rows.title: Working with the user and between sessions — Sessions
rows.summary: Several sessions may work in the tree at once.
body: Several sessions may work in the tree at once. One owns a project while it works on it; another asks it for a
change by message, or makes the change itself when the owner is not active and the user asks, and then updates
that project's documents.

rows.title: Working with the user and between sessions — The user
rows.summary: PHP developer, author of CodeBuilder, new to Rust and compilers.
body: PHP developer, author of CodeBuilder, new to Rust and compilers. Writes in Spanish: **the chat is always in
Spanish**, step by step, with concrete examples from the project (analogies with CodeBuilder are allowed in the
chat, never in the documents). Thinks of Nuclear like Elixir (modules, everything is a value, `if` and `match`
return) and prefers clear errors to inference by magic. Wants vivid, bright syntax colors.
Frequent mistakes in the Nuclear the user writes: comment lines without ` * ` (N0021), `title: x` in arguments
(it is `title = x`), `!` before a value (it is `not`; `x!` after a value exists), `const` and `new` (they do not
exist), indentation that is not 2 spaces.

rows.title: How the platform is tested
rows.summary: Rules:
body: Rules:
- A test that cannot find a folder of the tree fails; it never skips itself.
- A golden file changes only with `UPDATE_GOLDEN=1` and a review of the difference.
- A check that needs an SDK the machine lacks is listed as *Untested* in the project's roadmap, not left out.

rows.title: How the platform is tested
rows.summary: Each project's tests and how to run them are in its `AGENTS.md` and its `docs/05-standards/testing.md`.
body: Each project's tests and how to run them are in its `AGENTS.md` and its `docs/05-standards/testing.md`.
| Level | What it covers | Command (from the root) |
| Rust crates | the lexer, the parser, the resolver, the emitter, the loader, the language server, the command line tools; golden files of every dialect's examples | `cargo test` |

| The references | every Nuclear → target block of a dialect's reference is the transpiler's real output | `cd nuclearlang && tools/spec-check/check.py dialects/<language>/docs/07-reference/<dialect>.md <dialect> <language>` |
| The standard library | the same program prints the same in TypeScript, Dart and Python | `nuclearlang/tools/stdlib-check.sh` |
| A platform with a dialect | its example built, the target's analyzer in strict mode, its tests, a live run | `nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/<platform>/checks/` |
| The extensions | compile, the pipeline's and the set-up's tests, the bundled server loads every dialect | `extensions/vscode`: `npm run compile && npm test && npm run server` |
| The agents | a bank of tasks against a frontier model | `nuclear-agents/nuclear_developer/eval/run.py` |

- **The installation**: `installer/install.sh` → `~/.local/bin/{nuclear,synapsis,nuclear-lsp,nuclear-builder}`,

- **The AI services**: the systemd user units `nuclear-graph` and `nuclear-developer`

rows.title: Context documentation
rows.summary: The source of truth of the platform for people and AI agents.
body: The source of truth of the platform for people and AI agents. What a user reads (each project's references and
guides) is published at [nuclearlang.github.io](https://nuclearlang.github.io). This folder holds only what is about the **whole
platform**. Each project documents itself, in its own folder, the same way.

rows.title: Context documentation — How to read
rows.summary: 1. The root `AGENTS.md` is always loaded: the hard rules and the map of projects.
body: 1. The root `AGENTS.md` is always loaded: the hard rules and the map of projects.
2. Open the `AGENTS.md` of the one project the task touches. It lists that project's documents.
3. Open a document only when its line in that list matches the task. Never read a folder "to be safe".

rows.title: Context documentation — Rules
rows.summary: links to it.
body: - **One fact, one file, one project.** Another file links to it. A project never describes another project: it
links to it.
- **Short files.** A document is read in one go: over about 200 lines it is split by topic.
- **English** (the chat with the user is in Spanish).
- **Front-matter** on every document: `status` (`draft`, `accepted`, `deprecated`, `superseded`), `owner`,
`updated` (a date), `related` (paths).
- **Nothing invented.** What cannot be read from the code or the existing documents is written
`TODO(human): <the question>`.
- **Pending work** of a project is `docs/01-product/roadmap.md` of that project, with the sections it needs of:
*Half done*, *Untested*, *To decide with the user*, *Pending*. A done item is deleted. No file lists the pending
work of the whole platform.
- **Decisions.** Each project numbers its ADRs from 0001, in the format of `03-adr/0000-template.md`. An ADR is
cited with its project's key: `ADR-lang-0007`, `ADR-mobile-0002`. A change to a decision is a new ADR; the old
one is marked `superseded by ADR-<key>-NNNN`.
- **A feature** starts as a spec in the `04-specs/` of the project it changes; one that changes several projects
is here.
The layout is the user's (`05-standards/agent-context-docs-implementation.md`), with two layers added for a
language: `07-reference` and `08-guides`.

rows.title: Context documentation — What every project has
rows.summary: `AGENTS.md` at its root: what the project is, its stack, its commands, its folders, its own rules and the list of its documents with one line each saying when to read it.
body: `AGENTS.md` at its root: what the project is, its stack, its commands, its folders, its own rules and the list of
its documents with one line each saying when to read it. Under 150 lines. A `CLAUDE.md` beside it holds only
`@AGENTS.md`.
`README.md` beside it: the page a person reads first, on GitHub or in the folder. It is not `AGENTS.md` (that one
is for whoever changes the project) and it repeats no reference. Under the title, one line: the badge of each CI
workflow that tests the project (`https://github.com/nuclearlang/lang/actions/workflows/<file>.yml/badge.svg`, linked
to the workflow) and the link to its page on the website (`https://nuclearlang.github.io/...`). Then, in this order,
short enough to read in a minute (about 60 lines; the detail is in the guides it links):
1. **What it is**, in one or two sentences a newcomer understands.
2. **Why it exists**: the problem it solves for an agent or a person, and what it leaves out on purpose.
3. **How we made it**: the decisions that shape it and why, each linked to its ADR (`docs/03-adr/`); what it is
written in and, when it is a product, which tools made it (ADR-platform-0004). Only true and measured claims.
4. **Try it**: the shortest commands that show it working, with what they print or open.
5. **Where to read next**: its guides (`docs/08-guides/`), its reference, its `AGENTS.md` to change it.

rows.title: ☢ NuclearLang
rows.summary: Dart and Python by declarative dialects.
body: **Write only the logic.** A minimal language made for AI agents and easy for people to read, built to TypeScript,
Dart and Python by declarative dialects. **Synapsis**, its framework, makes mobile apps, backends and web apps from
the same Nuclear.
[**nuclearlang.github.io**](https://nuclearlang.github.io) · [the repository](https://github.com/nuclearlang/lang) ·
[CI](https://github.com/nuclearlang/lang/actions)

[![website](https://github.com/nuclearlang/lang/actions/workflows/website.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/nuclearlang/lang/actions/workflows/website.yml)

| [**lang**](https://github.com/nuclearlang/lang) | Everything, in one repository: the language and its compiler, the dialects, Synapsis and its three platforms, the `nuclear` command, the code generator, the MCP server, the editors (VS Code, Cursor, Android Studio, IntelliJ, Zed), the Smart Graph, the local agents, the installers and the website |
